approach: As a narrative review, the authors synthesize existing literature by categorizing the interactions into three main neural subsystems: Central Nervous System (hypothalamic nuclei, HPA axis), Autonomic Nervous System (sympathetic and parasympathetic), and Sensory Nervous System. They analyze mechanisms involving specific metabolites (e.g., SCFAs, bile acids, neurotransmitters), signaling pathways (e.g., TLR2, β2-AR, CGRP), and immune cell modulation. The review also integrates clinical and preclinical evidence on immunotherapy responses and microbiota-based interventions (FMT, probiotics, microbiome engineering).

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides a comprehensive framework linking gut microbiota to cancer neuro-immunity across CNS, ANS, and sensory systems, detailing specific molecular mechanisms (metabolites, receptors, signaling pathways).

key_findings.conditions: Central Nervous System / Circadian Rhythm & HPA Axis
key_findings.finding: Gut microbiota dysbiosis disrupts circadian rhythms (via SCN) and HPA axis function, leading to altered melatonin secretion and elevated glucocorticoids. This promotes an immunosuppressive microenvironment by inhibiting dendritic cell maturation, expanding Tregs/MDSCs, and enhancing tumor invasion via EMT.

Microbiota-derived metabolites (e.g., LPS) can activate the sympathetic nervous system, increasing norepinephrine (NE) release. NE acts on β2-adrenergic receptors to promote M2 macrophage polarization, recruit MDSCs, suppress CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity, and induce resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy.

Microbial SCFAs activate vagal afferents, promoting acetylcholine release. ACh acts on tumor cells via mAChRs (promoting proliferation via PI3K-AKT/Wnt) and immune cells via nAChRs (inducing M2 macrophages and Tregs), facilitating immune evasion and perineural invasion.

Microbial metabolites (e.g., butyrate, DCA) modulate nociceptive neurons, influencing cancer-related pain and tumor progression. For instance, butyrate induces M1 macrophages that activate TRPV1 channels, while CGRP from sensory neurons suppresses NK cell function and promotes PDAC progression.

Specific microbiota (e.g., Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium) are associated with better responses to ICIs. Microbiota influences ICI efficacy via neuro-immune pathways, such as metabolite-mediated T cell remodeling and vagus-enteric neural reflexes. FMT from responders can restore sensitivity to ICIs in resistant models.

problem_or_question: To address the knowledge gap regarding the relationship between gut microbiota and cancer neuro-immunity, specifically how these systems interact to regulate tumor progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance, and to summarize the regulatory mechanisms and potential interventions.
research_scope: The review focuses on the bidirectional interactions between the gut microbiota and cancer neuro-immunity in the context of tumorigenesis, progression, and immunotherapy response. It covers central nervous system (CNS), autonomic nervous system (ANS), and sensory nervous system pathways, as well as microbiota-based interventions like FMT, probiotics, and engineered bacteria.
work_summary: This article systematically reviews the complex interplay between the gut microbiota and the cancer neuro-immune axis. It elucidates how gut microbiota and its metabolites modulate tumor phenotypes via neural pathways (central, autonomic, and sensory) and immune regulation, while also describing how tumors alter gut microbiota composition through neuro-immune feedback loops. The paper further explores how these mechanisms influence the efficacy of immunotherapies, particularly immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), and discusses potential microbiota-based interventions to enhance treatment outcomes and manage adverse events.
